topics.topic: Backup encryption envelope, key derivation, authentication, and key-identifier construction
questions: What exact authenticated-encryption construction and file envelope must every backup use, and which metadata is covered by authentication?
How is the backup-key identifier computed and encoded, and must it resist use as an offline verifier for candidate keys?
What exact authenticated-encryption and key-digest construction must a release use so that encryption, tamper detection and key identification are testable and interoperable?

What exact authenticated-encryption format is required, how is an arbitrary configured backup key converted to an encryption key, how are nonces generated, which metadata is authenticated, and which digest identifies the key?

quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
judgement.why: This is the same question about the backup envelope, authenticated encryption, key representation and key identifier already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Backup encryption format, authentication, key representation, and key-digest construction
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Cross-session import locking scope, protection, acquisition order, and atomicity
questions: Does the new instance lock intentionally override A13 by blocking uploads and confirmations from other owner sessions?
What locking rule makes the import’s cross-session file clearing atomic and deadlock-free relative to uploads, confirmations, confirmation-page creation and sign-out?
In what order are the instance lock and owner-session locks acquired, and must an accepted import lock every affected session before clearing its file?

Which lock protects an uploaded file when another session's accepted import clears it, in what order are the instance and session locks acquired, and may mapping or confirmation-step rendering read the file without the instance lock?

quotes:
The requests of one owner session that change its state — showing a
   confirmation step, uploading a file, a submission, a sign-out — are
   applied one at a time, in the order in which they take the session's one
   lock, after passing the session check:

An accepted import drops the
   uploaded file of every owner session (M11); a confirmation shown in
   another session is refused because the import is closed (rule 8).

Uploads
   and import confirmations of all sessions take one lock of the instance,
   one at a time, so no upload lands after the import that closed it.
judgement.divergence: One implementation acquires the instance and affected session locks in a fixed order, so mappings, uploads, confirmations and cross-session clearing are serialized; another lets mapping or confirmation rendering read session files outside the instance lock, so it can render or retain a file concurrently cleared by another session's accepted import, which the owner notices through the displayed mapping, retained upload or subsequent refusal.
judgement.why: The texts require both per-session and instance-wide serialization but do not define their composition for the import's cross-session mutation.

topics.topic: Metadata and validation semantics for an empty audit log in a backup
questions: What metadata value and validation rule represent an empty audit log?
What value is recorded and what check is performed when the audit log is empty?
What value is recorded and what check is performed when the audit log is empty, and does “last sequence” mean the greatest surviving entry or the separate never-reused sequence counter?

quotes:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number it holds and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the store's own integrity check
   passes and that its audit log ends at the recorded sequence number, and
   removes it; a backup that passes is renamed to its kept name, one that
   fails is deleted.
judgement.why: This is the same empty-audit-log backup-metadata question already assigned to State 6.

topics.topic: Syntax, encoding, and structural well-formedness rules for configuration items
questions: For every configuration item, which textual or binary encodings are accepted, and exactly which values fail the well-formedness check?
What exact syntax, encoding and structural conditions make each configuration item well formed?

What syntax, encoding and type rules make each configuration item well formed, including how an environment string's length is measured in bytes and whether secrets may contain arbitrary Unicode or encoded binary data?

quotes:
The configuration is the set of environment variables whose names begin
   with `REGISTRY_`, set as R0-23 says; no other variable is read or
   checked.
judgement.why: The accepted encodings, syntax and structural field types of configuration values are contract and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Backup scheduling behavior after forward clock jumps across scheduled times
questions: After a forward clock jump, does Registry run once for the current date, run once for every crossed date, or treat all crossed scheduled instants as missed?
Does such a jump cause one run for the current date, one run for every crossed date, or no run because those scheduled instants were missed?

quotes:
Every day at
   03:00 UTC, while Registry runs with its service tokens, it
   makes one backup run; a 03:00 that finds Registry stopped, or in an
   owner-only start (rule 9), makes no run, and none is made later in its
   place.

A run is made for a UTC date only when the running process sees the
   clock pass 03:00 of that date and no kept backup of that date exists, so
   a restart, a start at 03:00 or a clock set back makes no second run.
judgement.divergence: After a forward jump, one implementation makes one backup for the current UTC date, while another treats every crossed 03:00 as missed or runs once for every crossed date; the owner notices different backup dates, run counts and recovery freshness.
judgement.why: The scheduling rule defines ordinary passage through 03:00 and backward-clock behavior but leaves forward jumps across one or more scheduled instants open.

topics.topic: Canonical byte representation used for secret length and equality checks
questions: On which canonical byte representation are the 32-byte minimum, distinctness and constant-time comparisons performed?
How are environment-variable secret values converted to bytes for the length, equality and constant-time comparison checks?

quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
judgement.why: This is the same question about the encoded byte representation used for secret length and equality checks already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Encoding used to measure and compare environment-variable secrets
quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
precedent.why: The textual or binary representation, decoding, equality and byte-counting rules for credential fields are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Durable tracking of failed daily backup attempts across restarts and clock rollback
questions: After a failed run, how is a prior attempt remembered across a clock rollback or restart so that the same UTC date cannot run twice?
What state records that a date's 03:00 run was already attempted when the attempt kept no backup, and does that state survive a process restart or a backward clock change?

quotes:
A run is made for a UTC date only when the running process sees the
   clock pass 03:00 of that date and no kept backup of that date exists, so
   a restart, a start at 03:00 or a clock set back makes no second run.

A step that fails leaves no partial kept backup —
   at most a file under the temporary prefix, which the next run removes —
   and writes a diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17);
   Registry keeps serving, and the next 03:00 tries again.
judgement.divergence: One implementation durably records the failed attempt and suppresses another run for that UTC date after restart or clock rollback; another relies only on the absence of a kept backup and runs again when 03:00 is crossed, which the owner notices through extra backup attempts, diagnostics and possibly a newly kept backup.
judgement.why: The rule promises no second run after restart or clock rollback but gives no verifiable state that preserves that behavior when a failed run leaves no kept backup.

topics.topic: Exact environment-variable names for configuration items
questions: What are the exact accepted `REGISTRY_` variable names, so Registry can distinguish required items from unknown ones?
What exact environment-variable names correspond to the store location, backup location, backup key, owner credential and four service tokens?

quotes:
The configuration is the set of environment variables whose names begin
   with `REGISTRY_`, set as R0-23 says; no other variable is read or
   checked.

It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).
judgement.why: Exact environment-variable field names are configuration-schema and contract details owned by State 6.
